summary: Defines managed objects for IP Flow Information Export, so that IPFIX exporters and collectors can be monitored, including their basic configuration. It is no longer current, because it was replaced by RFC 6615.

eli5.summary: It lists the dials used to watch machines that count network traffic. It was later replaced by a newer list.

subtitle: SNMP objects for monitoring IP flow exporters and collectors.

tldr.problem: Network administrators need to monitor the performance and configuration of devices that export IP flow data (traffic patterns).
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines SNMP MIB objects that let administrators watch and configure IPFIX exporters and collectors, including their transport connections, templates, and filtering.
tldr.outcome: Network equipment vendors can provide standardized management interfaces for traffic monitoring systems, and it was later superseded by RFC 6615.

facts.label: Main tables
facts.value: 7 (Transport Session, Template, Export, Metering Process, Observation Point, Selection Process)

facts.label: Information elements per template
facts.value: Variable; includes size and type information

facts.label: Timeout parameters
facts.value: Active timeout and inactive timeout for flow expiration

today: RFC 5815 was published as a Proposed Standard in April 2010 and defined the first IPFIX monitoring MIB. It was superseded by RFC 6615 with updates and corrections.

sections.title: Introduction to IPFIX Monitoring
sections.content:
The IP Flow Information eXport (IPFIX) protocol lets network administrators see what kind of traffic flows across their networks: the source and destination addresses, ports, protocols, and counts of bytes and packets for each conversation. IPFIX Exporters (devices on the network that measure traffic) send this data to IPFIX Collectors (analysis systems that receive and store it).

This document defines a set of SNMP MIB objects—data points that network management stations can read and write using the Simple Network Management Protocol—so that administrators can monitor both the exporters sending the data and the collectors receiving it. The MIB provides configuration dials for the connection between exporter and collector, the templates that describe the data format, and controls for filtering and sampling the traffic.

This RFC assumes that devices follow the IPFIX architecture defined in RFC 5470 and that the actual flow measurements and export happen according to RFC 5101. The document focuses on the monitoring and basic configuration aspects, not on the detailed configuration of how flows are measured.
sections.eli5: IPFIX watches network traffic. This defines dials and gauges so a network manager can check how those traffic watchers are working and tune them.

sections.title: The Structure of the IPFIX MIB
sections.content:
The IPFIX MIB is built around seven main tables. The Transport Session table is the foundation: it lists each connection between an exporter and a collector, including the protocol (TCP, UDP, or SCTP), the source and destination addresses and ports, and the status of the connection. For example, an exporter might have one TCP connection to collector A and one UDP connection to collector B.

The Template table lists all the data templates (format descriptions) that are sent or received on each transport session. Templates define which information elements (data fields like bytes sent or packet count) are included in the data records. The Template Definition table goes deeper, listing each field in a template, including the field's ID, its size, and whether it is used for filtering (scoping) or as a flow key.

The Export table shows which templates are exported from which metering processes (the traffic-measurement functions) to which transport sessions. This table supports failover and load-balancing: one metering process can export to multiple collectors, with some marked as primary backup copies, others for load-balancing.

The Metering Process table describes each traffic-measurement instance, including the observation point (e.g., an interface or tap) where traffic is measured and the timeout values that determine when a flow expires. The Observation Point table groups observation points together. The Selection Process table defines packet filtering and sampling functions that reduce the data volume before export.
sections.eli5: The MIB has shelves of data. One shelf is the connections (Transport Sessions). Another is the templates saying what data goes in each message. Others are metering (measuring), observation (where to measure), and selection (which packets to watch).

sections.title: Transport Sessions and Data Templates
sections.content:
Each transport session captures the network path between exporter and collector: the IP addresses, port numbers, and transport protocol. For TCP and UDP, the table stores source and destination IP addresses and ports. For SCTP (Stream Control Transmission Protocol), it stores the SCTP association ID instead, referencing the SCTP MIB module for details.

The transport session also tracks the IPFIX version being used and refresh parameters for templates on unreliable transports like UDP. On unreliable connections, templates must be resent periodically: the MIB can configure timeouts (how many seconds between resends) and refresh packet counts (how many data packets between resends).

Templates describe the format of the data records being exported. Each template has a unique ID within an observation domain (a logical grouping of measurement points). The same exporter can send different templates on different transport sessions or on the same session, and each template specifies a different set of information elements. For example, one template might include source IP, destination IP, and byte count, while another includes port numbers and flow timing.
sections.eli5: Each connection lists who talks to whom and on what port. Templates on that connection say which data fields each message will contain, and on slow connections, when to send them again.

sections.title: Metering and Observation Points
sections.content:
The Metering Process is the function that measures traffic flows. A device can have multiple metering processes, each with its own cache of active flows. Flows expire when they have been idle for too long or have been active for too long, controlled by the inactive and active timeout values. The MIB lets administrators set these timeouts to control how long flows are remembered before being exported.

Metering processes can be associated with Observation Points—the locations where traffic is measured. An observation point might be a physical interface on a router, a virtual interface, or a traffic tap. The Observation Point table groups these into logical sets; a metering process can reference a group of observation points to indicate where its flows are measured.

The Selection Process table represents packet filtering and sampling functions that can reduce the amount of data exported. For example, a selection process might sample only 1 in 1000 packets, or might filter to export only traffic on certain ports. The IPFIX SELECTOR MIB (a separate but related MIB module) defines standard selection functions that can be referenced by this table.
sections.eli5: Metering watches traffic and remembers flows for a set time. Observation Points are the taps—interfaces or links being watched. Selection Processes filter and sample to reduce data.

sections.title: Monitoring and Management
sections.content:
The MIB is designed to be read and written via SNMP, the standard protocol for network management. A network management station can query these objects to see which exporters and collectors are active, what templates they are using, which transport sessions are connected, and so on.

Most MIB objects MUST be implemented, reflecting the core IPFIX architecture. Some objects MAY be implemented depending on the device's capabilities—for example, a device that does not support SCTP does not need to populate SCTP-related fields.

The document references the ENTITY MIB and the IF MIB (Interface MIB), which provide information about physical and logical interfaces. IPFIX monitoring integrates with these existing management standards so that administrators can correlate flow data with interface state, hardware inventory, and other managed objects.
sections.eli5: A management computer asks the IPFIX device "Tell me what connections are active" and "Change the flow timeout from 100 seconds to 50." The MIB defines the questions and answers.
